# The Hansen--Hurwitz Estimator (UPSWR)


## How to Do Unequal Probability Sampling? {.smaller}

Suppose $n>1$ and we sample **with replacement**: the selection probabilities do not change after the first
draw. Let
$$
\psi_i = P(\text{select unit } i \text{ on any given draw}),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i=1 .
$$

Draw $n$ units with replacement (a unit may be drawn more than once). The sample $\mathcal R$ (not $\mathcal S$)
is the list of the $n$ draws, **including repeats**: for example, $n=10$, $$\mathcal R=\{D,D,D,C,C,D,C,A,B,B\}$$ 
A common choice, **probabilities proportional to size (PPS)**, with a size variable $x_i>0$ known for every unit:
$$
\psi_i = \frac{x_i}{t_x},\qquad t_x=\sum_{k=1}^N x_k .
$$

## Drawing Probabilities in Practice

```{r}
#| label: fig-pps-line
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| out-width: "85%"
set.seed(1)
psi <- c(0.10, 0.22, 0.15, 0.28, 0.25)
labels <- LETTERS[1:5]
cum <- c(0, cumsum(psi))
draws <- c(0.06, 0.35, 0.55, 0.83)

par(mar = c(3, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "", bty = "n")
cols <- rep(c("#dbe9fb", "#c3dbf7"), length.out = 5)
rect(cum[-6], 0.3, cum[-1], 0.7, col = cols, border = "black", lwd = 1.5)
text((cum[-6] + cum[-1]) / 2, 0.5, labels, cex = 1.4)
axis(1, at = cum, labels = round(cum, 2), cex.axis = 0.9)
points(draws, rep(0.5, 4), pch = 17, col = "firebrick", cex = 1.8)
text(draws, rep(0.82, 4), sprintf("u=%.2f", draws), col = "firebrick", cex = 0.85)
```

Divide $[0,1]$ into segments of length $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_N$. Draw $u\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)$ (red triangles);
the segment that $u$ falls into determines the selected unit. In R:
`sample(1:N, size = n, prob = psi, replace = TRUE)`.

## Ratios $b_i$ and the Ratio $B$

With $\psi_i=x_i/t_x$, define for every unit
$$
b_i=\frac{y_i}{x_i},\qquad B=\frac{t_y}{t_x}=\frac{\bar y_U}{\bar x_U},\qquad \bar x_U=\frac{t_x}{N}.
$$
$B=\sum x_ib_i/\sum x_i$ is the $x$-weighted mean of the $b_i$, and
$$
\bar y_U=\bar x_U\,B,\qquad t=t_x\,B .
$$
**Estimating $B$ is enough**: build $\hat B$, then multiply by $\bar x_U$ or $t_x$.

## Sampling Distribution of $b_j^*$

Let $b_j^*$ be the ratio $b$ of the unit selected on draw $j$ (the star: it is indexed by the *draw*, so it is
random, while $b_1,\ldots,b_N$ are fixed numbers). It is a discrete random variable with distribution

| Unit selected on draw $j$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\cdots$ | $N$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Value of $b_j^*$ | $b_1$ | $b_2$ | $\cdots$ | $b_N$ |
| Probability | $\psi_1=x_1/t_x$ | $\psi_2=x_2/t_x$ | $\cdots$ | $\psi_N=x_N/t_x$ |

Draws are with replacement, so $b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*$ are **IID** with this distribution.

## Mean and Variance of $b_j^*$

$$
E(b_j^*)=\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i\,b_i=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{x_i}{t_x}\frac{y_i}{x_i}=\frac{t}{t_x}=B,\qquad
S_{b^*}^2=V(b_j^*)=\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i(b_i-B)^2 .
$$
A single draw is unbiased for $B$, and precise when the $b_i$ are nearly equal, i.e. $y_i\propto x_i$.

## HH Estimator of $B$: Mean and Variance

The HH estimator is the mean of the $n$ IID observations $b_j^*$ (the **mean of the ratios**):
$$
\boxed{\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar b^*=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n b_j^*},\qquad E(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=B,
$$
and its variance is that of one draw divided by $n$:
$$
V(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{S_{b^*}^2}{n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i(b_i-B)^2 .
$$
No finite population correction: the draws are independent.

## Estimating the Variance; Mean and Total

The sample variance of the $b_j^*$ is unbiased for $S_{b^*}^2$:
$$
\boxed{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{s_{b^*}}{\sqrt n}},\qquad
s_{b^*}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n(b_j^*-\bar b^*)^2 .
$$

| Quantity | Estimate | Estimated SE |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Ratio $B=t/t_x$ | $\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |
| Mean per unit $\bar y_U=\bar x_UB$ | $\bar x_U\,\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $\bar x_U\,s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |
| Total $t=t_xB$ | $t_x\,\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $t_x\,s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |

## HH Estimator in Terms of $\psi_i$

**From $\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$** (PPS, $\psi_i=x_i/t_x$, so $t_x/x_i=1/\psi_i$):
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}&=t_x\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}\\
&=t_x\,\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n b_j^*\\
&=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n t_x\frac{y_j^*}{x_j^*}\\
&=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*}
\end{aligned}
$$

## The Weight of the HH Estimator

Writing the sum over the draws in $\mathcal R$ (repeats included):
$$
\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}=\frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal R}\frac{y_i}{\psi_i}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal R}w_i\,y_i,
$$
$$
\boxed{w_i=\frac{1}{n\,\psi_i}}
$$

* Each term $y_i/\psi_i$ is an estimate of the total $t$; the information about $t_x$ is carried in $\psi_i$.
* This holds for **any** selection probabilities $\psi_i$.
* Unit $i$ is expected to appear $n\psi_i$ times, so each draw of unit $i$ **represents** $1/(n\psi_i)$ units.
* With PPS, $w_i=t_x/(n\,x_i)$: large units get small weights.

## Variance of the HH Estimator in Terms of $\psi_i$ {.smaller}

**From $V(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=S_{b^*}^2/n$**, using $t_xb_i=y_i/\psi_i$ and $t_xB=t$, so that
$t_x(b_i-B)=y_i/\psi_i-t$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
V(\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}})&=t_x^2\,V(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i\,t_x^2(b_i-B)^2\\
&=\boxed{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i\Big(\frac{y_i}{\psi_i}-t\Big)^2}
\end{aligned}
$$
Likewise $t_x(b_j^*-\bar b^*)=y_j^*/\psi_j^*-\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}$, so the estimated variance
$t_x^2s_{b^*}^2/n$ is
$$
\hat V(\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}})=\boxed{\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{j=1}^n\Big(\frac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*}-\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}\Big)^2}
$$
Both hold for **any** $\psi_i$, with no finite population correction.

## Equivalence: $\psi_i$ as a Normalized Size

Take the **normalized size** $\tilde x_i=\psi_i$, so that $t_{\tilde x}=\sum_i\tilde x_i=1$ and
$\tilde x_i/t_{\tilde x}=\psi_i$. Its ratios and population ratio are
$$
\tilde b_i=\frac{y_i}{\tilde x_i}=\frac{y_i}{\psi_i},\qquad \tilde B=\frac{t}{t_{\tilde x}}=t ,
$$
so the HH estimator of $\tilde B$ is the HH estimator of the total:
$$
\hat{\tilde B}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*}=\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}},\qquad
\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}=t_{\tilde x}\,\hat{\tilde B}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\hat{\tilde B}_{\mathrm{HH}} .
$$

* With a normalized size, the "ratio" **is** the total.
* Conversely, $\psi_i=x_i/t_x$ gives $y_j^*/\psi_j^*=t_x\,b_j^*$, so $\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}=t_x\,\bar b^*$.
* Rescaling a size variable to total 1 does not change the estimator of the total.


# Example: Revenue from AI Token Usage

## Setup and Sample 

An AI company has $N=6$ customers; the tokens $x_i$ (millions) are known for all, the revenue $y_i$
(thousand dollars) is only observed for the sampled customers. Draw $n=5$ customers with replacement,
$\psi_i=x_i/t_x$ ($t_x=100$, $\bar x_U=16.67$). The sample is $\mathcal R=\{F,E,F,D,C\}$:

| Draw $j$ | Customer | $x_j^*$ | $y_j^*$ | $b_j^*=y_j^*/x_j^*$ | $b_j^*-\bar b^*$ | $(b_j^*-\bar b^*)^2$ |
|:--:|:--:|--:|--:|----:|----:|----:|
| 1 | F | 40 | 190 | 4.7500 | $-0.1417$ | 0.020069 |
| 2 | E | 30 | 155 | 5.1667 | 0.2750 | 0.075625 |
| 3 | F | 40 | 190 | 4.7500 | $-0.1417$ | 0.020069 |
| 4 | D | 15 | 70 | 4.6667 | $-0.2250$ | 0.050625 |
| 5 | C | 8 | 41 | 5.1250 | 0.2333 | 0.054444 |
| **Sum** | | | | **24.4583** | 0 | **0.220833** |

## Estimates 

$$
\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar b^*=\frac{24.4583}{5}=4.8917,\qquad
s_{b^*}^2=\frac{0.220833}{4}=0.0552,\quad s_{b^*}=0.235
$$

| Quantity | Estimate | Estimated SE |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Revenue per million tokens $B$ | $4.8917$ | $0.2350/\sqrt5=0.1051$ |
| Mean revenue per customer | $16.67\times4.8917=81.53$ | $16.67\times0.1051=1.75$ |
| Total revenue | $100\times4.8917=489.2$ | $100\times0.1051=10.5$ |

In R, with the sample as a data set `token` (one row per draw, columns `y` and `x`), `upswr_est` returns
the estimate, SE and CI; `method` is `"ratio"`, `"mean"` or `"total"`:

```r
upswr_est(token$y, token$x, xbar_pop = 100 / 6, tx_pop = 100, method = "total")
upswr_est(token$y, token$x / 100, xbar_pop = 1 / 6, tx_pop = 1, method = "total")  # x = psi
```

Both give $\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}=489.2$ (SE $10.5$): the second uses the normalized size $\tilde x_i=\psi_i$.

## Physicians: HH Estimates and SRS Comparison {.smaller}

With the population in thousands, $b_j^*$ = physicians per 1,000 people of the county on draw $j$:

| Quantity | HH estimate | SE |
|:---|--:|--:|
| Physicians per 1,000 people, $\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | 2.24 | 0.16 |
| Physicians per county, $\bar x_U\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | 181.6 | 13.2 |
| Total physicians, $t_x\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | 570,304 | 41,401 |

Compared with estimates from a separate SRS of 100 counties (`counties.csv`):

| Method | Estimate | SE | Estimate $-$ true |
|:---|--:|--:|--:|
| Sample total $N\bar y$ (SRS) | 933,411 | 491,983 | 400,773 |
| Ratio estimator (SRS) | 639,506 | 87,885 | 106,868 |
| Regression estimator (SRS) | 585,871 | 105,177 | 53,233 |
| Hansen--Hurwitz (UPSWR) | 570,304 | 41,401 | 37,666 |

Using the size at the **design** stage (HH) gives the smallest SE here; the next section explains when.

# Comparison of the HH, Ratio and Average Estimators of the Total

## Three Estimators of the Total {.smaller}

Residuals about the line through the origin:
$$
d_i=y_i-Bx_i,\qquad B=\frac{t}{t_x},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^N d_i=0 .
$$

* **Sample average** (SRS, ignores $x_i$): $\hat t_{\mathrm{avg}}=N\bar y$,
  $\displaystyle V(\hat t_{\mathrm{avg}})=\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{N^2S_y^2}{n}$.
* **Ratio** (SRS, $x_i$ at the estimation stage): $\hat t_r=t_x\,\bar y/\bar x$; an SRS selects every unit with
  probability $1/N$, so
  $$
  V(\hat t_r)\approx\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac{N^2S_d^2}{n}\approx\Big(1-\frac nN\Big)\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{d_i^2}{1/N}.
  $$
* **HH** (UPSWR, $x_i$ at the design stage, $\psi_i=x_i/t_x$): each draw deviates by a scaled residual,
  $$
  \frac{y_i}{\psi_i}-t=\frac{d_i}{\psi_i}
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  V(\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{d_i^2}{\psi_i}.
  $$

## Comparison of the Three Estimators

| Estimator | Estimator of $t$ | Variance | $x_i$ used at | Unbiased? |
|:---|:--:|:--:|:---|:---|
| Sample average (SRS) | $N\bar y$ | $\Big(1-\dfrac nN\Big)\dfrac{N^2S_y^2}{n}$ | not used | yes |
| Ratio (SRS) | $t_x\,\dfrac{\bar y}{\bar x}$ | $\approx\Big(1-\dfrac nN\Big)\dfrac1n\sum\limits_{i=1}^N\dfrac{d_i^2}{1/N}$ | estimation stage | slightly biased |
| HH (UPSWR) | $\dfrac1n\sum\limits_{j=1}^n\dfrac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*}$ | $\dfrac1n\sum\limits_{i=1}^N\dfrac{d_i^2}{\psi_i}$ | design stage | exactly unbiased |

: {tbl-colwidths="[17,13,40,15,15]"}

For the mean, divide the estimators by $N$ and the variances by $N^2$.

## On a Common Scale {.smaller}

Ignoring the fpc, each variance is $\frac1n\sum_i$ (squared deviation)/(selection probability of unit $i$):

| Estimator | Term of unit $i$ | Spread of $y$ about |
|:---|:--:|:---|
| Sample average | $\dfrac{(y_i-\bar y_U)^2}{1/N}$ | the flat line $\bar y_U$ |
| Ratio | $\dfrac{d_i^2}{1/N}$ | the line $y=Bx$ |
| HH | $\dfrac{d_i^2}{\psi_i}$ | the line $y=Bx$ |

* **Ratio vs average:** $y_i-\bar y_U=d_i+B(x_i-\bar x_U)$. If $y\approx Bx$, the ratio estimator removes the spread
  due to $x$; if $y$ is unrelated to $x$, $d_i$ *adds* it and the average wins.
* **HH vs ratio:** the same $d_i^2$, divided by $\psi_i$ instead of $1/N$. Units with $\psi_i>1/N$ (larger than
  average) are **downweighted**, since they are already drawn more often.

## When Does UPS Beat the Ratio Estimator? {.smaller}

$$
V(\hat t_r)-V(\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}})\approx\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^N d_i^2\Big(N-\frac1{\psi_i}\Big)
=\frac Nn\sum_{i=1}^N d_i^2\Big(1-\frac{\bar x_U}{x_i}\Big),
$$
so HH wins exactly when the units with large residuals are larger than average:
$$
\boxed{H_d=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N d_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^N d_i^2/x_i}>\bar x_U}
$$
If $d_i^2\approx\sigma^2x_i^{\gamma}$:

| Spread of $y$ about the line $y=Bx$ | $\gamma$ | Better |
|:---|:--:|:---|
| constant | $0$ | ratio (SRS) |
| $\mathrm{SD}\propto\sqrt{x}$, i.e. $V(y_i)\propto x_i$ | $1$ | tie |
| $\mathrm{SD}\propto x$: constant coefficient of variation | $2$ | HH (UPSWR) |

: {tbl-colwidths="[60,10,30]"}

Revenues, acreages and counts often have a roughly constant CV ($\gamma\approx2$): PPS works well for them.

## Three Population Shapes

```{r}
#| label: ups-spread-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "100%"
plot_ups_spread()
```

Plot $y$ against $x$ (census or pilot): if the scatter **fans out** in proportion to $x$, sample with PPS; if its
width stays about the same, use an SRS with the ratio estimator.

```{r toy-functions}
#| include: false
# one-draw variances of the three estimators of t: N (y_i - ybar_U)^2, N d_i^2, d_i^2 / psi_i
toy_table <- function(x, y) {
  N <- length(x)
  B <- sum(y) / sum(x)
  psi <- x / sum(x)
  d <- y - B * x
  tab <- data.frame(Store = LETTERS[1:N], x = x, y = y, psi = psi, d = d,
                    avg = N * (y - mean(y))^2, r = N * d^2, h = d^2 / psi)
  rbind(tab, data.frame(Store = "**Variance** (Sum)", x = sum(x), y = sum(y), psi = sum(psi),
                        d = sum(d), avg = sum(tab$avg), r = sum(tab$r), h = sum(tab$h)))
}
show_toy_table <- function(tab)
  knitr::kable(tab, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 4, 2, 1, 1, 1), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
               col.names = c("Store", "$x_i$", "$y_i$", "$\\psi_i$", "$d_i=y_i-Bx_i$",
                             "$N(y_i-\\bar y_U)^2$", "$N\\,d_i^2$", "$d_i^2/\\psi_i$"))
x_toy <- c(100, 200, 300, 1000)
```

## Toy Example: Four Supermarkets {.smaller}

Floor areas $x_i$, $t_x=1600$, $\psi_i=x_i/t_x$ against $1/N=0.25$ in an SRS; $t=300$, $B=0.1875$.
One-draw variances (the sum of each column). **Sales proportional to floor area:**

```{r toy-good}
show_toy_table(toy_table(x_toy, c(11, 20, 24, 245)))
```

Store D has the largest residual and $\psi_D=0.625>1/N$: HH divides $d_D^2$ by $0.625$ instead of $0.25$.
HH $<$ ratio $\ll$ average; here $H_d=529>\bar x_U=400$.

## Toy Example: Sales Unrelated to Floor Area {.smaller}

The same stores and the same total $t=300$, but the sales hardly vary:

```{r toy-bad}
show_toy_table(toy_table(x_toy, c(60, 80, 90, 70)))
```

The ordering reverses: the line $y=Bx$ fits badly, all the $d_i$ are large, and the ratio estimator and HH are
more than 30 times worse than the sample average. **The size variable must be tied to $y$.**

## Simulation and App

* **Simulation** (book, Section 7.3.3): 2000 samples of 300 counties from `agpop`, $y$ = acres in 1992,
  $x$ = acres in 1987. The naive SRS total has a huge variance; the SRS ratio and regression estimators and
  UPSWR remove most of it.
* **App:** [SRS (average and ratio) with UPSWR and UPSWO](../shinylives_sampling/app-ups.html){target="_blank"}
  reports the simulated and theoretical variance reductions relative to the plain SRS average.

# One-Stage Cluster Sampling with PPS

## Change of Notation

Clusters (psus) are the units: $y_i\to t_i$ (cluster total), $x_i\to M_i$ (cluster size),
$$
t_x\to M_0=\sum_{i=1}^NM_i,\qquad \bar x_U\to\bar M_U=\frac{M_0}{N},\qquad \psi_i=\frac{M_i}{M_0}.
$$
The ratio of cluster $i$ is its **mean per element (ssu-level mean)**
$$
b_i=\frac{t_i}{M_i}=\bar y_i ,\qquad B=\frac{t}{M_0}=\bar y_U\ \ (\text{mean per element}).
$$

## Estimates for One-Stage Cluster Sampling

Then $\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=\dfrac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\bar y_j^*$: the **plain average of the sampled cluster
means** (large clusters are already selected more often), with $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=s_{\bar y^*}/\sqrt n$,
$s_{\bar y^*}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_j(\bar y_j^*-\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}})^2$.

| Quantity | Estimate | Estimated SE |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Mean per element $\bar y_U=t/M_0$ | $\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $s_{\bar y^*}/\sqrt n$ |
| Mean per cluster $\bar t_U=t/N$ | $\hat{\bar t}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar M_U\,\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $\bar M_U\,s_{\bar y^*}/\sqrt n$ |
| Total $t$ | $\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}=M_0\,\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $M_0\,s_{\bar y^*}/\sqrt n$ |

In R, `cluster_upswr(ti, Mi, N, M0, estimate)` calls `upswr_est` with $y=t$, $x=M$, and reports in this
notation; `estimate` is `"ybar"`, `"tbar"` or `"total"`.

## Example: Falls in Long-Term Care Homes 

$N=40$ homes, $M_0=3000$ residents ($\bar M_U=75$). $n=8$ draws with $\psi_i=M_i/M_0$; every resident of a
selected home is reviewed ($t_i$ = falls in the home). Home H12 is drawn twice (same $t_i$):

:::: {.columns}

:::{.column style="width:58%;"}

| $j$ | Home | $M_j^*$ | $t_j^*$ | $\bar y_j^*=t_j^*/M_j^*$ |
|:--:|:--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | H12 | 180 | 160 | 0.8889 |
| 2 | H03 | 60 | 49 | 0.8167 |
| 3 | H27 | 240 | 205 | 0.8542 |
| 4 | H12 | 180 | 160 | 0.8889 |
| 5 | H31 | 95 | 70 | 0.7368 |
| 6 | H08 | 120 | 118 | 0.9833 |
| 7 | H19 | 45 | 30 | 0.6667 |
| 8 | H36 | 150 | 140 | 0.9333 |
| **Sum** | | | | **6.7688** |

:::

:::{.column style="width:42%;"}

$\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}=6.7688/8=0.8461$ falls per resident, $s_{\bar y^*}=0.1036$,
$\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=0.1036/\sqrt8=0.0366$.

| Quantity | Est. | SE |
|:---|--:|--:|
| per resident $\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | 0.846 | 0.037 |
| per home $\hat{\bar t}_{\mathrm{HH}}$ ($\times75$) | 63.5 | 2.7 |
| total $\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}$ ($\times3000$) | 2538 | 110 |

:::

::::

## Falls in Care Homes with `cluster_upswr` {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r falls-cluster-upswr}
#| echo: true
home <- c("H12", "H03", "H27", "H12", "H31", "H08", "H19", "H36")
Mi <- c(180, 60, 240, 180, 95, 120, 45, 150)
ti <- c(160, 49, 205, 160, 70, 118, 30, 140)
res <- cluster_upswr(ti, Mi, N = 40, M0 = 3000, estimate = "total", cluster = home)
res$table
res$estimate |> format_est_gt("hh_total")
```

# Two-Stage Cluster Sampling with Replacement

## Setup and Estimators

Select $n$ clusters with replacement, $\psi_i=M_i/M_0$, then take an SRS of $m_i$ elements from the cluster
**on every draw**: a cluster drawn twice gets two **independent** subsamples. The cluster mean $b_i=t_i/M_i$ is
not observed, but estimated by the subsample mean $\bar y_i$, and $\hat t_i=M_i\bar y_i$.

The one-stage formulas carry over with $\bar y_j^*$ now the subsample mean of draw $j$:
$$
\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\bar y_j^*,\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{s_{\bar y^*}}{\sqrt n},\qquad
s_{\bar y^*}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n(\bar y_j^*-\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}})^2 ,
$$
mean per cluster $\hat{\bar t}_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar M_U\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}$ and total $\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}=M_0\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}$ with SEs multiplied by the same constants
(each draw estimates the total by $\hat t_j^*/\psi_j^*=M_0\bar y_j^*$).

::: {.callout-note}
**No second-stage variance formula is needed**: the draws are independent, and $s_{\bar y^*}^2$ captures both the
choice of clusters and the choice of elements within them.
:::

## Example: Care Homes with Subsamples 

Same eight draws, but $m_j^*=20$ residents are sampled per draw (15 for H19), recording their falls. H12 is
drawn twice, with different subsample means:

:::: {.columns}

:::{.column style="width:58%;"}

| $j$ | Home | $M_j^*$ | $m_j^*$ | Falls | $\bar y_j^*$ |
|:--:|:--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | H12 | 180 | 20 | 19 | 0.950 |
| 2 | H03 | 60 | 20 | 15 | 0.750 |
| 3 | H27 | 240 | 20 | 16 | 0.800 |
| 4 | H12 | 180 | 20 | 16 | 0.800 |
| 5 | H31 | 95 | 20 | 18 | 0.900 |
| 6 | H08 | 120 | 20 | 21 | 1.050 |
| 7 | H19 | 45 | 15 | 10 | 0.667 |
| 8 | H36 | 150 | 20 | 17 | 0.850 |
| **Sum** | | | | | **6.767** |

:::

:::{.column style="width:42%;"}

$\hat{\bar y}_{\mathrm{HH}}=6.767/8=0.846$, $s_{\bar y^*}=0.120$, $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=0.120/\sqrt8=0.0425$.

| Quantity | Est. | SE |
|:---|--:|--:|
| per resident | 0.846 | 0.042 |
| per home ($\times75$) | 63.4 | 3.2 |
| total ($\times3000$) | 2538 | 127 |

:::

# Unequal Probability Sampling Without Replacement (UPSWO)

## The Horvitz-Thompson Estimator

Select $n$ **distinct** units with **inclusion probabilities** $\pi_i=P(i\in\mathcal S)$, $\sum_{i=1}^N\pi_i=n$.
For $\pi$ps, $\pi_i=n\,x_i/t_x=n\psi_i$. The **Horvitz-Thompson (HT)** estimator weights each unit by $1/\pi_i$:
$$
\boxed{\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}}
$$
*Unbiased*: with $I_i=1$ if $i\in\mathcal S$ (and $E(I_i)=\pi_i$), $\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}=\sum_{i=1}^N I_i\,y_i/\pi_i$ and
$$
E(\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}})=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}E(I_i)=\sum_{i=1}^N y_i=t .
$$

## Mean and Ratio from the HT Total

Mean per unit: $\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}/N$. With $\pi_i\propto x_i$, the ratio is the HT total over $t_x$:
$$
\hat B_{\mathrm{HT}}=\frac{\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}}{t_x}=\frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}b_i ,
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat B_{\mathrm{HT}})=\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}})}{t_x}.
$$

## Variances of the HT Estimator

With joint inclusion probabilities $\pi_{ij}$ (fixed sample size), **Sen-Yates-Grundy**:
$$
\hat V_{\mathrm{SYG}}=\frac12\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}\frac{\pi_i\pi_j-\pi_{ij}}{\pi_{ij}}\Big(\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}-\frac{y_j}{\pi_j}\Big)^2 .
$$
Approximations that need only $\pi_i$, with $u_i=y_i/\pi_i$:

* **Hájek**: $\displaystyle\hat V_{\mathrm H}=\frac{n}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(1-\pi_i)(u_i-A)^2,\quad
A=\frac{\sum_{\mathcal S}(1-\pi_i)u_i}{\sum_{\mathcal S}(1-\pi_i)}$
* **With-replacement (WR)**: treat the sample as $n$ draws with $\psi_i=\pi_i/n$,
$\displaystyle\hat V_{\mathrm{WR}}=\frac{n}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\Big(u_i-\frac{\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}}{n}\Big)^2$,
which ignores the factors $1-\pi_i$ and is a little too large.

For the mean divide the SE by $N$; for $\hat B_{\mathrm{HT}}$ divide by $t_x$.

## Example: HT Estimate and Variances {.smaller}

$N=20$ units, a sample of $n=4$ units with inclusion probabilities $\pi_i$:

| $i$ | $y_i$ | $\pi_i$ | $u_i=y_i/\pi_i$ | $(1-\pi_i)u_i$ | $(1-\pi_i)(u_i-A)^2$ | $(u_i-\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}/n)^2$ |
|:--:|--:|--:|------------:|------------:|----------------------:|-----------------:|
| 1 | 12 | 0.10 | 120.00 | 108.00 | 17.08 | 12.8 |
| 2 | 30 | 0.20 | 150.00 | 120.00 | 526.1 | 698.5 |
| 3 | 40 | 0.35 | 114.29 | 74.29 | 65.9 | 86.2 |
| 4 | 33 | 0.30 | 110.00 | 77.00 | 144.3 | 184.2 |
| **Sum** | | | **494.29** | **379.29** | **753.4** | **981.6** |

$\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}=494.29$, mean $494.29/20=24.71$; $A=379.29/3.05=124.36$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat V_{\mathrm H}&=\tfrac43\times753.4=1004.5\ (\mathrm{SE}=31.7),\\
\hat V_{\mathrm{WR}}&=\tfrac43\times981.6=1308.8\ (\mathrm{SE}=36.2).
\end{aligned}
$$
SE of the mean: $31.7/20=1.58$ (Hájek), $36.2/20=1.81$ (WR).

# When to Use UPS

## UPS Is Risky Unless $y$ Is Tied to the Size Variable

The gain depends on the residuals $d_i=y_i-Bx_i$ being small, i.e. $y_i$ roughly proportional to $x_i$; UPS
beats the SRS ratio estimator only when the spread about the line grows with the size ($H_d>\bar x_U$).
Otherwise,

* the estimate can be **much worse than a plain SRS average**;
* a unit with small $x_i$ but large $y_i$ gets a huge weight $1/\psi_i$ ($1/\pi_i$), so the estimates are unstable and
  the estimated SE tends to be too small (intervals under-cover).

UPS is used mostly when the size is a good proxy of what is measured: selecting the clusters of a multi-stage
survey proportional to households or students, auditing by monetary value, surveys of establishments by
employment. If the size is only loosely related to $y$, use SRS or stratified sampling, with a ratio or
regression estimator if $x_i$ is known.
